name: The World of AI: Power and Cooling Section on Datacenter Electricity
title: The World of AI: Power and Cooling Section on Datacenter Electricity
answer: The World of AI's Power and Cooling section is a short, curated page with three entries on how AI datacenters get electricity and shed heat. Its most useful point is a DOE 2024 LBNL figure: datacenters used about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023, projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028, with AI as the driver. The page frames this as a hard constraint on AI scaling, because grid growth may lag compute demand.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this page as a section of its AI ecosystem atlas, under Technology and Core Infrastructure. It is a short landing page for Power and Cooling, not a full report. The page says it holds three power and cooling entries, each curated with a verified vendor or primary source and re verified daily. Its stated scope is how an AI datacenter gets electricity and gets rid of heat, including grid connection and interconnection queues, generation contracted to serve the load, and the shift from air to liquid cooling that dense GPU racks forced. It says individual facilities are in Data Centers, while racks and interconnect are in other hardware sections. The page was retrieved on 2026-09-27 and says every page is rebuilt daily and carries the date it was last verified. It also includes site search details, book promotions, consulting services, and audit product names.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page's substantive claim is that datacenter electricity demand is rising from about 4.4% of US consumption in 2023 to a projected 6.7 to 12% by 2028, driven primarily by AI workloads, according to the Department of Energy's 2024 analysis. It attributes this to DOE's 2024 LBNL report. The page says this trajectory reflects a hard constraint on AI scaling. The grid cannot expand as fast as compute demand grows. Even modest adoption of AI training and inference at scale will require either new generation capacity, storage, or load shifting, none of which are built yet. The range of the projection, 6.7 to 12%, signals uncertainty about how fast AI deployment actually happens, which depends on factors the electricity numbers alone cannot capture. The section also says it covers grid connection and interconnection queues, the generation contracted to serve the load, and the shift from air to liquid cooling that dense GPU racks forced. It notes that individual facilities are in Data Centers, and the racks and interconnect inside them are in other hardware sections. The page further describes the wider site as an atlas of artificial intelligence covering state AI laws, a lawsuit tracker, a glossary, a tools directory, AI companies, a research library, an MCP server registry, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators, and weekly digests, all built from the same database and rebuilt daily from primary sources. It also promotes books by Stephen R. Jordan, a novel called The AI Lawyer, and several consulting audit services.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that datacenters consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and are projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028, citing the Department of Energy's 2024 analysis and DOE's 2024 LBNL report. It says AI is the driver. It says the section has three power and cooling entries, each curated with a verified vendor or primary source and re verified daily. It states that the grid cannot expand as fast as compute demand grows, that even modest adoption of AI training and inference at scale will require new generation capacity, storage, or load shifting, and that none of these are built yet. It says the 6.7 to 12% range signals uncertainty about how fast AI deployment happens. It also says the site is free to read, free to cite, and free to query.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in Energy can use this source as a short, citable pointer to the DOE datacenter electricity projection and to the power constraint framing. It is useful for tracking the demand side of AI, the grid connection and interconnection queue issue, the generation contracted to serve datacenter load, and the move from air to liquid cooling. It also places those topics in a wider AI atlas with laws, lawsuits, glossary, tools, companies, research, MCP servers, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators, and weekly digests. Because the page is brief and cites DOE rather than reproducing the full report, it works best as an entry point or reference note, not as a standalone analysis of energy markets or grid planning.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Energy

sections.body: This is a short section landing page with only three entries, not the DOE report itself. It does not give the DOE report's methodology or any regional breakdown, generation mix, or facility level detail. It says individual facilities are covered in Data Centers and racks and interconnect in other hardware sections, so this page is partial by design. It is partly commercial, because it promotes books, a novel, and consulting audit services. It is dated by retrieval on 2026-09-27 and says pages are rebuilt daily, but the core figures come from a 2024 analysis using 2023 data, so the numbers are not current to the retrieval date. It also does not state a publication date for the page itself.
